subject: Specifying a location dependent tau and kappa, with a user generated function

messages.author: 4f6838d1ceab9ca6
messages.subject: Specifying a location dependent tau and kappa, with a user generated function
parts:
Hello,
         I have been following the example in Section 2.3.2 of the SPDE tutorial (http://www.r-inla.org/examples/tutorials/spde-tutorial) which shows how R-INLA can handle a non-stationary covariance, by making the parameters tau and kappa as location dependent. 

In that example, tau is set to be tau_i = exp( theta_1 + theta_3 * sin(pi*x) ) where x is the spatial location (Pg 53).

Here the preexisting sin(x) function in R is used to represent the non-stationarity. However, I would like to employ a user defined function, because tau in my problem depends on the output of another simulation package. I would like to try the following solution:

1) Read in the external field which specifies tau.
2) Build a function in R which evaluates this field at an arbitrary point using an interpolation approach.
3) Pass this function to the spde object in R-INLA.

Would such an approach result in any issues/incompatibility ?

Thanks.
--
Vikram Garg
Postdoctoral Associate
The University of Texas at Austin

http://vikramvgarg.wordpress.com/
http://www.runforindia.org/runners/vikramg

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Specifying a location dependent tau and kappa, with a user generated function
parts:
It depends on precisely which mathematical model you want to implement.

Any log-linear model is fine, where your own function is used as a “covariate”,
and where it is smooth enough to be well approximated on the triangle domain.
In this case this would simply feed straight into the B.tau and B.kappa matrices.

If you need a more general nonlinear parameterisation, you’d need to use an rgeneric model construction that explicitly constructs the precision matrix using your own tau and kappa, and the output from inla.mesh.fem() (or some other method for constructing the precision)

If you can give more details on how your user defined function depends on parameters that are to be estimated by inla, it will be easier to give more specific advice.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Specifying a location dependent tau and kappa, with a user generated function
parts:
Hello Dr. Lindgren,
                              I can provide a little more context about the problem I am trying to solve. My objective is to generate samples from a distribution with a non-stationary covariance. The specific parameter being modeled is a turbulent mixing parameter that arises in ocean dynamics, and hence we have a large problem size and spatially varying structure, handling which requires INLA's capabilities.

We would like to model the non-stationary covariance of the turbulent mixing parameter as follows. From our ocean model, we will output the pointwise norm of the bathymetry gradient ( norm_b_grad(s) ) over the region of interest. The INLA parameter kappa (~local correlation length) will be set as:

kappa(s) = exp(constant - norm_b_grad(s) ), 

whereas the parameter tau (~local marginal variance) will be set as.

tau(s) = exp(constant + norm_b_grad(s) )

Regarding the smoothness of norm_b_grad(s), it is the norm of the gradient of a C0 piecewise linear function, and hence is itself a discontinuous piecewise constant function, i.e. not particularly smooth. 

Thanks.

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Specifying a location dependent tau and kappa, with a user generated function
parts:
OK, so if I interpret that correctly, you have _known_ constant
offsets, and _no_ parameters that need estimating? Not even
multipliers like
kappa(s) = exp(theta[1] - theta[3] * norm_b_grad(s))
tau(s) = exp(theta[2] + theta[3] * norm_b_grad(s))
?

The piecewise constantness of norm_b_grad is basically ok; you may
want to have some odd behaviour at the discontinuities, but that's
hard to avoid.

First, project norm_b_grad onto the triangulation, to give
norm_b_grad_on_mesh. Exactly how to do that has several possibilities.

The most basic is to evaluate the function at the mesh nodes:
for (k in seq_len(nrow(mesh$loc)))
norm_b_grad_on_mesh[k] <- norm_b_grad(mesh$loc[k, ])

Another option, that will give nicer behaviour at the continuities, is
to approximate a projection based on integrals over the triangles.
Let s_k and w_k be some numerical integration scheme points and
weights, and let phi_k(s) be the triangular basis functions,
and let z(s) be norm_b_grad(s).

One could consider building the approximation from the point of view
of the mesh, by "pulling" information at the individual points onto
the mesh, like when evaluating z(s) at the mesh nodes, see above.

For high-resolution covariates as input to kappa and tau (global
elevation map) the most robust method I've used has been this simple
weighting (it's not quite the full least-squares projection, but
rather something simpler and more local) that is mare akin to
"pushing" the information onto the mesh.

int_domain psi_k(s) z(s) ds / int_domain psi(s) ds
\approx
sum_k w_k psi_k(s_k) z(s_k) / sum_k w_k psi_k(s_k)

An additional benefit of this approach is that it's much easier to
implement; let w_k = 1, and place s_k in a dense lattice covering the
domain, let's call them integ_loc:

integ_loc <- ... ## expand.grid or inla.mesh.lattice, for example.
integ_A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=integ_loc) ## Computes psi_k(s_k)
integ_z <- ... ## Evaluate norm_b_grad at the integ_loc points
z_on_mesh <- as.vector(integ_A %*% z) / rowSums(integ_A)

The parameterless model is simply given by (in the inla.spde2.matern call)

B.kappa = matrix(constant_kappa - z_on_mesh, mesh$n, 1)
B.tau = matrix(constant_tau + z_on_mesh, mesh$n, 1)

This just specifies a known offset in the log-scale.

With parameters (see beginning of message):

B.kappa = cbind(0, 1, 0, -z_on_mesh)
B.tau = cbind(0, 0, 1, +z_on_mesh)

Hopefully this should get you going a bit?

Finn
